actions: assists elbow extension, stabilizes elbow (dynamically tensions the joint capsule)

functional_compartments.name: Single fiber population
functional_compartments.function_note: Small triangular muscle continuous with triceps' medial head; active throughout elbow extension to protect the joint capsule from impingement.

trigger_points.location_description: In the muscle belly just distal and posterior to the lateral epicondyle, between the epicondyle and the olecranon
trigger_points.referred_pain_pattern: A small, focal pattern over the lateral epicondyle
trigger_points.activation_perpetuating_factors: Forceful extension and pronation; associated trigger points in triceps (especially medial head), supinator, and wrist extensors
trigger_points.notes: Produces lateral epicondylar pain resistant to extensor-origin treatment; case reports describe an 'anconeus syndrome' of lateral elbow pain relieved by treating the muscle; differentiate from pain referred into this region from triceps TrP1/TrP2, supinator, brachioradialis, ECRL/ECRB, extensor digitorum, supraspinatus, posterolateral plica, radial head pathology, or posterolateral rotatory instability

clinical.compiled_by: repository owner (physician); elbow_muscles_reference_v2.html, compiled 04/09/2026 (v2; v1 31/08/2026). Strength data come from the Mayo elbow series (An et al. 1981; Askew et al. 1987), from MRI/cadaver architecture studies (Murray et al. 2000; Kawakami et al. 1994) and from Neumann (2017). Values are population means; individual variation is large.
clinical.function_biomechanics: EMG shows anconeus active in extension at every speed, but its torque contribution is small (Murray: ~2–3 cm² PCSA, short moment arm). Its functionally distinct roles are (1) abduction of the ulna during pronation about an axis through the index finger, keeping the hand centred (Gleason 1985; the longitudinal fibres are more active in pronation than supination, Bergin 2013); (2) dynamic lateral stabilisation, compressing the humero-ulnar joint and resisting varus and posterolateral rotatory displacement, hence the description as an "active lateral ligament" (Molinier 2011); and (3) tensioning the posterolateral capsule to prevent it being pinched in the olecranon fossa. Its precise contribution to pronation kinematics remains debated (lidocaine-blocking studies found minimal effect).
clinical.adjacent_structures: Adjacent bursae: None intrinsic; the subcutaneous olecranon bursa lies medial to it. Adjacent structures and relations: Lateral ulnar collateral ligament and annular ligament deep; radial head and capitellum antero-deep; ECU and supinator anteriorly; posterior interosseous nerve emerging distal to supinator, well anterior.

trigger_points.location: In the muscle belly just distal and posterior to the lateral epicondyle, between the epicondyle and the olecranon.
trigger_points.referred_pain: a small, focal pattern over the lateral epicondyle.
trigger_points.notes: Symptoms / mimics: Lateral epicondylar pain resistant to extensor-origin treatment; pain with forceful extension and pronation. Case reports describe an "anconeus syndrome" of lateral elbow pain relieved by treating the muscle. Entrapment: None. Associated TrPs: Triceps (especially medial head), supinator, wrist extensors.
trigger_points.source: Travell & Simons, vol. 1, 2nd ed., 1999: ch. 32 (anconeus with triceps).

clinical.pain_referred_into_territory: Pain referred INTO this region from elsewhere
clinical.notes: Pedicled anconeus flap covers lateral soft-tissue defects and salvages failed lateral epicondylitis surgery; the Kocher (anconeus–ECU) and Boyd approaches use its borders. Its medial-sided variant, anconeus epitrochlearis, is described in the variants section.
clinical.caveat: Clinical reference for professional use; anatomical variation is frequent and trigger-point patterns describe typical, not universal, presentations. Referred pain is presented in both directions: pain that each muscle's TrPs refer to other regions, and pain that other muscles (shoulder, chest, back) and non-muscular sources refer into the elbow region. Where Travell & Simons did not map a muscle separately (extensor digiti minimi, pronator quadratus) this is stated rather than filled in.
